遥感如何发现热带森林的“隐蔽毁林”？

How does remote sensing reveal 'hidden' tropical deforestation?

除肉眼可见的皆伐外，高分辨率与时间序列影像能识别零星采伐、林冠退化与道路侵入等缓慢变化，结合雷达可穿透云层，捕捉传统统计遗漏的小规模破坏。
Beyond clear-cuts, high-resolution time-series and radar see through clouds to catch sporadic logging, canopy degradation and road incursion—slow changes missed by conventional statistics.

卫星“日光诱导叶绿素荧光（SIF）”能告诉我们什么？

What does satellite solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) tell us?

SIF 是植物光合过程中逸出的微弱红光，直接反映真实光合作用强度，比叶面积指数更早指示干旱、物候与碳吸收的变化。
SIF is faint red light leaking from photosynthesis, directly tracking actual photosynthetic activity—earlier than leaf-area indexes at signaling drought, phenology and carbon uptake changes.

合成孔径雷达（SAR）为何能“全天候”监测地表形变（如地面沉降）？

Why can SAR monitor surface deformation (e.g., subsidence) all-weather?

SAR主动发射微波、接收回波，不受云雨黑夜影响；用干涉（InSAR）比对两时相相位差，可毫米级测出地面升降，广泛用于沉降、滑坡、冰川流速监测。
SAR actively emits microwaves and receives echoes, unaffected by clouds, rain or night; interferometry (InSAR) compares phase between dates to measure uplift/subsidence at millimeter scale—used for subsidence, landslides and glacier velocity.

卫星如何用“大气柱 CO2 浓度”来追踪排放源？

How do satellites track emission sources via 'column CO2 concentration'?

如 OCO-2、GOSAT 等用光谱反演大气柱平均 CO2，叠加风场可定位羽流并估算电厂、城市等点源的排放量，弥补地面监测的空白。
Satellites like OCO-2 and GOSAT retrieve column-average CO2 from spectra; with wind data they pinpoint plumes and estimate emissions from power plants or cities, filling ground-monitoring gaps.

卫星遥感如何监测全球森林变化？

How does satellite remote sensing monitor global forest change?

光学与雷达卫星定期成像，通过植被指数（如NDVI）、雷达穿透云层，结合AI比对前后影像，识别砍伐、恢复与火灾范围，实现近实时全球覆盖。
Optical and radar satellites image regularly; vegetation indices (e.g., NDVI) and cloud-penetrating radar, combined with AI change detection, identify deforestation, regrowth and fires at near-real-time global coverage.

卫星怎么“看到”森林被砍？

How can satellites 'see' forests being cut?

卫星拍下大地的颜色，森林是深绿；被砍后变成土黄，电脑一比前后照片就知道哪里变了。
Satellites photograph Earth's colors; forest is deep green, and after cutting it turns earthy yellow—computers compare before/after photos to spot changes.
